items.answer: Teleportation is a virtual reality locomotion operation in which a user selects a virtual target location and the virtual viewpoint instantly changes from the current location to that target, without physical movement.

Navigation is an interaction in an immersive virtual world that moves the user from one point to another by changing the user's viewpoint, mostly without object interaction, and has two components: locomotion and wayfinding.
Locomotion technique is a technique that lets a user travel in a virtual world from one place to another and perceive that travel has taken place.

Wayfinding is the component of navigation, other than locomotion or travel, that provides location awareness, ascertains a path to a destination, transfers spatial knowledge to the real world, and builds a mental model of the environment.

Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

questions.question: How were the broad goals of the Majuli VR tour translated into design work?
options: User experience design, island exploration, and cyber sickness handling
Video editing, image correction, and ambient sound mixing
Pilgrim content, student content, and tourist content
Headset selection, tracking setup, and software optimization
questions.explanation: The tour’s objectives of capturing heritage, enhancing presence, and minimizing cyber sickness were carried into design through user experience, exploration, and sickness handling. The other options are production or hardware tasks, not the design considerations framed by those goals.

questions.question: Why did the wide geographic spread of the Majuli VR tour require careful design?
options: Moving quickly between information points can make cultural videos hard to follow
Catering to several user groups can make the navigation too complex
A large, content-rich area can take enough time to cause cyber sickness
Showing the whole island can make the virtual environment too static
questions.explanation: A large, content-rich area increases the time needed to explore it, and that time can lead to cyber sickness if the design does not manage it. The other risks are not the design concern identified for the island’s spread.

questions.question: How did the Majuli VR tour development process continue after an initial design was made?
options: It asked users to compare the final layout with the island’s real locations
It kept one fixed design and added new cultural content after release
It first finished the full tour and then asked users to choose preferred paths
It cycled through design, prototype, and evaluation with user feedback
questions.explanation: The final design followed an iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle, refining ideas from user feedback and observations. A single late review or a fixed post-release design would not match that process.

questions.question: How did early observations of island visitors differ from later user feedback in shaping the Majuli VR tour?
options: Early observations added a minimap and controls, while later feedback chose the locations
Early observations shaped locations and groups, while later feedback added interface elements
Early observations replaced the prototype cycle, while later feedback added the notification system
Early observations set the final boat ride, while later feedback chose the user groups
questions.explanation: Observations of island visitors informed early choices such as which locations to cover and how to categorize users, while feedback and interaction later contributed design elements such as a minimap, notifications, and user controls. The first wrong option reverses those roles.

data.text: The Majuli VR tour's design was framed by goals of capturing heritage, supporting user presence, and reducing cyber sickness. The tour's large, content-rich geographic spread made careful design important, because extended exploration can lead to sickness. The final design was developed through the ISDL iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle, starting from guidelines and refining ideas with island visitor observations and user feedback. That user-informed process shaped choices about locations, user groups, and interface features.
points: The Majuli VR tour's design aimed to capture heritage, enhance user presence, and minimize cyber sickness.
The Majuli VR tour's large geographic spread can cause cyber sickness if its time-consuming exploration is not carefully designed.
The final Majuli VR tour design used the iterative ISDL design-prototype-evaluate cycle, starting from guidelines and refining with user input.
Observations of island visitors and user feedback shaped the Majuli VR tour's locations, user groups, and interface features.

questions.question: What determined the tailoring of the virtual tour's content and features?
options: the different preferences of the pilgrim, student, and tourist groups
the different entry points of the pilgrim, student, and tourist groups
the different hardware requirements of the pilgrim, student, and tourist groups
the different sickness risks of the pilgrim, student, and tourist groups
questions.explanation: The three user categories were distinguished because each had its own preferences for visiting or exploring the island, and the tour's content and features were tailored to those preferences. Hardware, sickness risk, and entry point were not the stated basis for the tailoring.

questions.question: What method, besides user interaction and user feedback, was used to identify the information points on the island?
options: environmental presence questionnaires on the island
simulator sickness questionnaires on the island
introductory videos from the island
field trips to the island
questions.explanation: The information points were identified using interaction with users, field trips, user feedback, and the need to cover the entire island. Questionnaires for sickness or presence and introductory videos were not the method used to identify the points.

questions.question: Why was the virtual tour designed to include all of the island's identified information points?
options: to reduce the travel time between sites on the island
to provide a separate route for each user category
to capture the tangible and intangible heritage of the whole island
to replace the multimedia archive of heritage information
questions.explanation: Covering all 24 information points allowed the tour to comprehensively capture the tangible and intangible heritage aspects of the entire island. It was not intended to shorten travel time, create separate category-specific routes, or replace a multimedia archive.

data.text: The Majuli virtual tour design began with identifying users and their preferences, so its content could suit different visitors. User interaction, field trips, feedback, and the need to cover the whole island then produced 24 information points. The tour covers those points to present the island's tangible and intangible heritage comprehensively.
points: The first stage of user experience design is identifying users so the experience can suit them.
The Majuli virtual tour's user categories were pilgrims, students, and tourists, and content was tailored to their contextual-inquiry preferences.
The island's information points were selected through user interaction, field trips, user feedback, and the need to cover it.
The island's 24 information points comprised 9 satras, 6 villages, and 9 towns or other important places.
The Majuli virtual tour covers all 24 points to capture the island's tangible and intangible heritage comprehensively.

questions.question: What do the opening videos shown on the curved screen provide to the user?
options: a heritage preview and a site map for the virtual tour
an island introduction and a system guide for the virtual tour
a presence questionnaire and a sickness scale for the virtual tour
a boat ride preview and a bank view for the virtual tour
questions.explanation: The starting point uses a curved screen to introduce the island and familiarize the user with how to use the system. The boat crossing is a separate transport metaphor, not the opening tutorial content.

questions.question: Why is a 360-degree boat ride video used at the very start of the virtual tour?
options: to provide a preview of the island's satras and villages
to show the island from a single fixed elevated view
to measure the user's sense of presence before entry
to give the feeling of being carried across a river
questions.explanation: The boat ride video simulates a crossing, making the user feel carried from one side of the river to the other. It is not a site preview, a fixed view, or a presence measurement.

questions.question: What does the user select before the actual virtual tour begins?
options: a visitor category shown with an icon
an information point shown with a map
a boat route shown with a timeline
a presence level shown with a slider
questions.explanation: Before the tour proper starts, the user chooses a user group, such as pilgrim, student, or tourist, represented by an icon. Selecting an information point, route, or presence level is not part of that initial selection.

data.text: The opening of the Majuli virtual tour creates an immersive context before the actual tour. It combines introductory and tutorial videos on a curved screen with a 360-degree boat-ride video that makes the user feel transported between mainland and island. The user then selects a user group, shown by pilgrim, student, or tourist icons, before the tour starts.
points: The virtual tour opens on a curved screen with introductory and tutorial videos about Majuli island and system use.
A 360-degree boat-ride video gives the feeling of crossing the river from mainland to island or island to mainland.
Before the tour, the user chooses a user group shown by pilgrim, student, or tourist icons.

questions.question: Why are unwanted elements such as a 360-camera tripod or its shadow removed during preprocessing?
options: to mark the original camera position
to reduce the media file size
to improve the visual appearance
to support the familiar interface
questions.explanation: Unwanted camera artifacts are removed so the scene looks cleaner and more natural. Removing them is not about file size, marking the camera, or making the interface familiar.

questions.question: Why are 360-degree images edited for uniform illumination?
options: to keep unwanted objects out when moving between images
to keep the frame rate high when moving between images
to keep the ambient sound steady when moving between images
to keep the lighting even when moving between images
questions.explanation: Uniform illumination prevents a sudden lighting change from feeling odd when the user moves from one 360-degree image to another. It is separate from object removal, sound placement, and performance tuning.

questions.question: What determines which ambient sound is played in the virtual tour?
options: the time of day recorded
the viewing direction selected
the user group chosen
the type of place visited
questions.explanation: Ambient sounds are matched to the kind of place being visited, such as temple bells for a satra or religious site. They are not chosen by capture time, user group, or viewing direction.

data.text: The tour's visual and audio material was prepared to establish an initial immersive context. Making the images and videos visually consistent reduces oddness when the user moves between captured places. Ambient sounds matched to each location further support realism and authentic ambience.
points: The collected 360-degree images and videos were preprocessed by using high-resolution content, making illumination uniform, and removing unwanted elements.
Ambient sounds were played depending on the place visited to enhance realism and authentic ambience.

questions.question: Which features belong to the navigation tools of the virtual tablet interface?
options: Info elements for place details and notifications for available cultural videos for wayfinding
A global map for the entire island and a local minimap at each spot for wayfinding
A volume controller and other controls for playing cultural videos for wayfinding
A left-side island map in miniature and buttons for opening the mini map for wayfinding
questions.explanation: The tablet's navigation tools are the miniature island map and the controls for opening the mini map. The local minimap belongs to the local interface, while video controls and info elements serve other purposes.

questions.question: What purpose does a video player on the virtual tablet interface serve?
options: Alerting users to available cultural videos or activities of a place
Viewing cultural videos or top-view drone videos of a place
Showing the island map or local minimap views of a place
Playing ambient sounds or temple bell audio of a place
questions.explanation: A video player on the virtual tablet interface is for viewing cultural or top-view drone videos. Ambient sounds and notifications are separate system features, and maps are not shown by such a player.

questions.question: Why is the virtual tablet interface designed to resemble a real-world tablet?
options: To make the island map compact for users
To make cultural videos simpler to watch for users
To make it familiar and easy for users
To make notifications clearer for users
questions.explanation: Resembling a real-world tablet makes the tablet interface familiar and easy for users to use. The other options name benefits of particular components, not the stated design reason.

data.text: The virtual tablet interface is the main interface given to users, and it brings together the tools needed for navigation and content access. Its miniature island map and mini-map buttons help users orient themselves, while its video player and info elements provide videos and information. The real-tablet-inspired design is meant to make these tools familiar and easier to use.
points: The virtual tablet interface provided to users acts as the main interface.
The virtual tablet interface's navigation tools include a left-side island map as a miniature world and mini-map opening buttons.
The virtual tablet interface's video player has a volume controller and other controls for cultural or top-view drone videos.
The virtual tablet interface provides access to information content through info elements.
The virtual tablet interface's design is inspired by real-world tablet use to make it familiar and easy.

questions.question: Why is a minimap at an information point used instead of only the whole-island map?
options: to reduce clutter and give clear local direction
to show the entire island with its complete layout
to track the user's pose and correct drift
to blend consecutive 360-degree images
questions.explanation: The local minimap focuses on one place, reducing clutter and giving clear direction for wayfinding. Showing the whole island in one view is the role of the global map.

questions.question: What do the white dots on a minimap indicate?
options: the available cultural video spots
the active information icon alerts
the virtual vehicle travel routes
the layout of 360-degree images
questions.explanation: White dots mark the layout of the 360-degree images, and the user moves from one image to another along those dots. They do not mark videos, alerts, or vehicle routes.

questions.question: What happens when a user selects an arrow in the tour?
options: a cultural video starts at the nearest available spot
the user moves along the image dots in that direction
the whole-island map opens for wider navigation
a top-view drone video switches to the current place
questions.explanation: An arrow indicates a direction, and selecting it moves the user along the sequence of 360-degree images. It does not open maps or start videos.

questions.question: When the information icon is active, what does selecting it show?
options: whether a cultural video is available at that spot
whether a local minimap is available at that spot
whether a virtual vehicle is available at that spot
whether a direction arrow is available at that spot
questions.explanation: An active information icon alerts the user to cultural video content at that spot, and selecting it shows whether that video can be played. It does not indicate minimaps, arrows, or vehicles.

data.text: The island tour’s interface helps users move through places and find relevant content. A place-specific minimap represents the place’s 360-degree images as dots, and arrows move the user between them, giving local direction and wayfinding support. Notifications and an active information icon add awareness of cultural videos, while the separate global and local maps keep navigation clear.
points: A minimap is a place-specific world-in-miniature map, different from the global island map.
White minimap dots show 360-degree images, the current image is green, and arrows move the user.
Notifications and an active information icon show whether a cultural video is available at a spot.
The global map and local minimap reduce clutter and support wayfinding and spatial orientation awareness.

questions.question: What does view interpolation prevent when a user moves from one 360-degree image to another?
options: A cybersickness effect from walking navigation
A random user movement between images
A slow long-distance movement across the island
A sudden visual jerk between images
questions.explanation: View interpolation blurs the boundaries between two 360-degree images so the transition feels smooth instead of sudden. Navigation arrows, vehicle travel, and walking-based navigation address other parts of the tour.

questions.question: Why does the island tour need a different travel technique from walking-based navigation for exploring the whole island?
options: Navigation arrows would direct the user to the next 360-degree image
The virtual vehicle would give a seated viewpoint during travel
View interpolation would make every image transition a blur
Walking would take a lot of time and could lead to cybersickness
questions.explanation: Walking is suitable for a single spot, but traversing the entire island by walking would be time-consuming and may induce cybersickness. The other options describe features of the tour, not the reason for a different travel technique.

questions.question: What kind of locomotion technique is the virtual vehicle travel method in the island tour?
options: An instantaneous technique that places the user at the ray-cast target
A selection-based technique that follows a pre-planned route to a chosen destination
A free-walking technique that lets the user move to any nearby spot
A continuous steering technique that controls the vehicle's heading with each ray cast
questions.explanation: The virtual vehicle method uses pre-planned routes: the user selects a destination, which selects the route, rather than walking freely, moving instantly to a target, or steering continuously. Ray casting is used to select the destination, not to control the vehicle moment by moment.

data.text: The island tour connects places with 360-degree images, and view interpolation plus navigation arrows make movement between them smooth and directed. Because walking the whole island would be slow and could cause cybersickness, a 3D virtual vehicle metaphor supports long-distance travel. Inside that metaphor, a seated viewpoint, changing scenes, and ray-cast destination selection on pre-planned routes turn travel into selection-based route movement.
points: In the island tour, 360-degree images are joined by view interpolation, which smooths transitions between places.
Navigation arrows guide users between 360-degree images, preventing random movement and supporting smooth exploration.
The virtual vehicle metaphor is a 3D vehicle model for long-distance island travel, avoiding slow walking and possible cybersickness.
The virtual vehicle technique uses a ray-cast destination choice to select pre-planned routes from a seated viewpoint with changing scenes.

questions.question: What does the spot video list on the tablet do when a user is at a spot in the virtual tour?
options: It lists the most popular videos in the virtual tour for the user to choose
It lists videos from a nearby spot in the island for the user to choose
It lists textual descriptions of the spot for the user to choose
It lists that spot's videos for the user to choose
questions.explanation: The tablet adds the material relevant to the current spot so the user can select from that spot's videos, which may be cultural or ecological. The list is not based on popularity, nearby spots, or textual descriptions.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the textual descriptions in the virtual tour?
options: To give the user a smooth transition between two 360-degree images
To give the user context about locations and spots
To give the user a selected destination for a pre-planned route
To give the user a seated viewpoint inside the virtual vehicle
questions.explanation: Textual descriptions function as informative notifications and descriptions that add context about places and significant spots. Smooth image transitions, vehicle viewpoints, and destination selection are separate design features.

questions.question: How do directional arrows and information icons help a user notice important elements in the environment?
options: Arrows indicate which way to move, and icons give further details
Arrows show a local map of the place, and icons start the virtual vehicle
Arrows smooth the transition between images, and icons select a destination route
Arrows list videos for the spot, and icons play the selected video
questions.explanation: Directional arrows guide movement toward points of interest, while information icons provide further details, mostly textual, so important elements are not overlooked. Maps, vehicle control, transitions, and video playback are not the roles of these point-of-interest cues.

data.text: The virtual tour's tablet supports content exploration by tying media and information to the user's current virtual location. It offers cultural and ecological videos and spot-specific video lists, and adds textual context about locations and significant spots. Directional arrows and information icons then direct attention to points of interest and supply details so important elements are not missed.
points: The virtual tour's tablet video player provides cultural and ecological videos for the user's current virtual location.
When the user reaches a spot, the tablet lists that spot's videos, letting them choose material for their user type.
Textual descriptions appear as informative notifications and descriptions, giving extra context about locations and significant spots.
Directional arrows guide users to points of interest, and information icons give mostly textual details so nothing important is overlooked.

questions.question: Which feature of joystick-based navigation or teleportation is intended to reduce discomfort?
options: Controlled movement that avoids abrupt changes
A pre-planned route chosen for a destination
A seated viewpoint inside a virtual vehicle
A blurred boundary between consecutive 360-degree images
questions.explanation: Joystick-based navigation or teleportation uses controlled movement, so it does not support abrupt movements that can cause discomfort. The other options describe vehicle or image-transition features, not joystick-controlled navigation.

questions.question: What must be chosen carefully in vehicular movement because it may cause cybersickness?
options: The seated viewpoint inside the vehicle
The route selected by the virtual vehicle
The direction of a ray casting interaction
The speed of the change of viewpoint
questions.explanation: In vehicular movement, the speed at which the viewpoint changes may cause cybersickness if it is not chosen carefully. The other options are vehicle or interaction details, not the stated speed-related risk.

questions.question: What is one benefit of consistent visual cues and smooth transitions in the system design?
options: A faster change of the vehicle's viewpoint
A better feeling and awareness of the place
A fixed seated viewpoint inside the virtual vehicle
A shorter walking path between spots
questions.explanation: Consistent visual cues and smooth transitions help maintain spatial orientation and give the user a better feeling and awareness of the place. They do not increase vehicle speed, create a seated vehicle viewpoint, or shorten walking paths.

data.text: The XR tour design reduces cybersickness by controlling movement and keeping the visual experience stable. Joystick-based navigation or teleportation avoids abrupt movement, and the speed of vehicular viewpoint change is handled carefully because a speed not chosen carefully may cause cybersickness. Consistent visual cues and smooth transitions also maintain spatial orientation, reduce anxiety and sensory conflicts, and help avoid severe long-term cybersickness.
points: The XR system’s joystick-based navigation or teleportation avoids abrupt movement, reducing cybersickness discomfort.
In vehicular movement, if the speed of viewpoint change is not chosen carefully, it may cause cybersickness.
Consistent visual cues and smooth transitions maintain spatial orientation, reduce anxiety and sensory conflicts, and help avoid severe long-term cybersickness.

questions.question: In immersive experience work, what does the term “design” refer to?
options: Hardware and display settings
Content and narrative
Code and implementation
Interface and interaction
questions.explanation: In immersive experience work, design means interface and interaction design rather than code design.

data.text: The topic is the scope of design in immersive experiences. It clarifies that design refers to shaping the interface and interactions, rather than designing code.
points: In immersive experience design, design means interface and interaction design, not code design.

items.reason: The virtual tour's identified user categories are pilgrims, students, and tourists, while island visitors are the broader potential users observed during requirement gathering.

questions.question: How do the global island map and the local minimap in the Majuli VR tour work together to support a user's location awareness and wayfinding?
questions.reference_answer: The global island map and the local minimap form dual maps: the island map shows the whole island as a world in miniature on the tablet, while the minimap shows a specific place on the local interface. This separation reduces clutter and gives clear navigation support. The minimap also gives local orientation and indicates direction, helping the user build a mental model and wayfind.

questions.question: Why did the Majuli VR tour use a virtual vehicle travel technique for long-distance movement rather than walking-based navigation across the island?
questions.reference_answer: Exploring the entire island with walking-based navigation would take a lot of time and may lead to cybersickness, so a different travel technique was required. The virtual vehicle gives the user a seated viewpoint inside the vehicle and changes the surrounding scenes as it moves to create motion. The user selects a destination by ray casting, and because the route is pre-planned, this is selection-based route selection rather than target selection or instantaneous movement.

questions.question: Why does the Majuli VR tour ask a user to choose pilgrim, student, or tourist before the virtual tour begins?
questions.reference_answer: The choice is needed because the tour distinguishes pilgrims, students, and tourists as distinct user groups, and each group has its own preferences for exploring the island. The user chooses one of these icons before the tour so the experience can be tailored to that user type. At each spot, the tablet interface adds and lists videos whose relevance is determined by the current location and the user type.
